questions.q: Why is latency between a service in Azure and a service in AWS typically higher and less predictable than latency between two services in the same Azure region?
options: AWS deliberately throttles all traffic destined for Azure
Azure VNets are incapable of routing traffic to any external network
Latency is identical in both cases as long as BGP is enabled
Cross-cloud traffic leaves one cloud's network and crosses a tunnel or meet-point into another's, adding hops neither cloud's SLA fully covers on its own
questions.explain: Same-region, same-provider traffic stays on infrastructure one cloud fully controls end to end; cross-cloud traffic adds a tunnel or meet-point hop that isn't covered the same way.

questions.q: What is the general shape of how both Azure and AWS price data transfer?
options: Both directions, inbound and outbound, are billed at the same flat per-gigabyte rate
Data transferred into the cloud is typically free; data transferred out (egress) is metered and billed
All data transfer is free regardless of direction, as long as it stays within one region
Only data transfer between two services owned by the same billing account is ever charged
questions.explain: Both clouds price data transfer asymmetrically: inbound is typically free, while egress — data leaving the cloud's network to anywhere external, including another cloud — is metered and billed per gigabyte.

questions.q: From AWS's perspective, how is a large response sent from AWS back to a caller in Azure classified for billing?
options: It is not billed at all because the destination is another cloud rather than the public internet
It is billed only if the AWS service involved is in a different AWS region than the VPC
It is billed as AWS egress, because Azure is simply an external network from AWS's point of view
It is billed as Azure egress, since Azure is the one receiving the data
questions.explain: Each cloud treats the other cloud as just another external network, so outbound traffic to it is billed as that cloud's own egress, regardless of how the connection was built.

questions.q: Why does a 'chatty' service pattern — fetching, enriching, and writing back across the cloud boundary repeatedly per request — become especially expensive?
options: It pays egress charges on every outbound-crossing leg, multiplied by how often that pattern repeats per request
Chatty patterns are only expensive if they use HTTP instead of a binary protocol
Egress charges only apply to the first cross-cloud call in any given session
Chatty patterns reduce total egress because each individual call transfers less data
questions.explain: Every outbound-crossing leg of a chatty, repeated pattern incurs its own egress charge, so the cost scales with how often the cross-cloud round trip happens, not just with total data volume.

questions.q: When a service's heaviest-volume callers are in one cloud and its data source is in the other, what does this lesson suggest as one real input into where the service itself should run?
options: The service should always run in whichever cloud has the lower published compute price
Placement should be randomized to average out latency across both clouds
Running the service near its heaviest-volume caller keeps high-frequency traffic local, pushing the cross-cloud leg to the lower-frequency side of the relationship
Data gravity and residency requirements should be ignored in favor of minimizing egress alone
questions.explain: Keeping the high-frequency caller relationship intra-cloud and pushing the cross-cloud leg to a lower-frequency path (like a periodic sync) is a real, though not the only, consideration in service placement.
